title: Glucose at 340 nm vs the Bedside Meter: Haematocrit and Other Strip Pitfalls
summary: Learn why NADH absorbance at 340 nm tracks the hexokinase glucose method, how bedside meters differ, and how haematocrit, oxygen, other sugars, triglycerides, uric acid and acetaminophen push meter readings high or low.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 28 Hits 3 and 9 and Trap 4. Checked against Wolfe 2024 (NADH vs NAD+ absorbance), Lacorn 2025 (hexokinase/G6PD reaction read at 340 nm), Finfer 2013, Ashar 2026, Erbach 2016 and Ginsberg 2009 (the last two read via a page-fetch tool) and Calhoun 2018. Qualifications: oxygen interference applies to glucose oxidase strips (rv-ch28-poct-oxygen-enzyme); acetaminophen interference is system-dependent and a newer CGM was designed to resist it (rv-ch28-cgm-acetaminophen); the reviewer’s mechanism for the haematocrit effect is simplified (rv-ch28-hct-mechanism). Not taught as fact: NADPH at 340 nm, 340 nm-decrease assays (ammonia, urea, ALT, AST), CK, lactate and triglyceride variants, tetrazolium/formazan, and calibrating personal meters against lab values. The NCBI Bookshelf StatPearls “Hexokinase Method” page was blocked (browser check / 403) and was not read.

objectives: Explain why the hexokinase glucose method is read as an absorbance increase at 340 nm.
Predict the direction of the haematocrit effect on a bedside glucose meter.
Match oxygen, other sugars, triglycerides, uric acid and acetaminophen interference to the strip chemistry and direction of error.

scenes.title: A meter reads 300
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: a severely anaemic inpatient (haematocrit 22%) has a bedside fingerstick glucose of 300 mg/dL. Two pathways on screen: the meter strip (whole blood, enzyme electrode) and the central laboratory analyser (plasma, hexokinase, light at 340 nm). Question token: “Treat now, or confirm first?”

cues.text: Invented case: a severely anaemic patient, haematocrit twenty-two percent, has a bedside glucose meter reading of three hundred.
Two very different measurements could answer the question: the meter strip at the bedside, and the laboratory analyser reading light at three hundred and forty nanometres.
Should you treat the number now, or confirm it first?

scenes.title: The laboratory reads glucose at 340 nm
scenes.altText: Schematic spectrum card: the reduced cofactor NADH absorbs strongly at 340 nm; the oxidised form NAD+ does not absorb at 340 nm (both absorb at 260 nm). Reaction card: glucose + ATP → glucose-6-phosphate (hexokinase); glucose-6-phosphate + NAD+ → 6-phosphogluconate + NADH (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase). NADH formed is equimolar to glucose converted, so absorbance at 340 nm RISES in proportion to glucose. Reference card: a central-laboratory hexokinase method on plasma is one of the reference methods bedside meters are checked against.

cues.text: Start with the light. The reduced cofactor, NADH, absorbs strongly at three hundred and forty nanometres. Its oxidised form, NAD plus, does not absorb there.
In the hexokinase method, hexokinase and ATP turn glucose into glucose-6-phosphate. Then glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase oxidises it, reducing the cofactor to NADH.
One NADH is made for each glucose converted, so absorbance at three hundred and forty rises in proportion to the glucose.
A central-laboratory hexokinase method is one of the reference methods that bedside meters are checked against.

scenes.title: The meter reads whole blood
scenes.altText: Meter card: a strip enzyme (glucose oxidase or glucose dehydrogenase) passes electrons to an electrode; the sample is capillary whole blood. Plasma card: venous plasma glucose is about 10–15% higher than whole-blood glucose, so most meters convert to a plasma-equivalent value using correction factors; many meters are still affected by haematocrit. Haematocrit card: low haematocrit (below about 35%) tends to give falsely HIGH readings; high haematocrit gives falsely LOW readings. Red cells carry their own glucose and can block the electrode or enzyme. Example: true glucose 80 mg/dL at haematocrit 0.25 → positive bias up to about 18 mg/dL. Meters that correct for haematocrit are less susceptible.

cues.text: The meter works differently. A strip enzyme, glucose oxidase or glucose dehydrogenase, passes electrons from glucose to an electrode, and the sample is whole blood, not plasma.
Plasma glucose runs about ten to fifteen percent higher than whole-blood glucose, so meters convert to a plasma-equivalent value using correction factors.

Even so, many meters are still affected by haematocrit. Low haematocrit, below about thirty-five percent, tends to read falsely high; high haematocrit reads falsely low. Red cells carry glucose of their own, and they can block the electrode or the enzyme.

One consensus review gives an example: at a true glucose of eighty and a haematocrit of zero point two five, the bias can reach about plus eighteen. Meters that correct for haematocrit are less susceptible.

scenes.title: What else fools a strip
scenes.altText: Interference table. Glucose oxidase strips: oxygen competes with the mediator for electrons — high pO2 (patient on oxygen) → falsely low; low pO2 → falsely high. Glucose dehydrogenase strips: little affected by oxygen, but other sugars (galactose, xylose, maltose) can compete. Icodextrin from peritoneal dialysis can raise readings by more than 100 mg/dL and has been reported with both strip types. Any electrochemical strip: very high triglycerides take up volume → falsely low; very high uric acid oxidised at the electrode → falsely high; acetaminophen can give falsely high readings in some electrochemical meters and older continuous glucose monitors; hypotension with poor perfusion can lower capillary glucose. Hook answer card: anaemia pushes a meter high — confirm with a laboratory plasma glucose before acting; one evaluation concludes point-of-care glucose suits monitoring rather than definitive diagnosis.

cues.text: Glucose oxidase strips are sensitive to oxygen, which competes for the electrons. A patient on oxygen can read falsely low; a very low oxygen tension can read falsely high.

Glucose dehydrogenase strips are little affected by oxygen, but other sugars such as galactose, xylose and maltose can compete. Icodextrin from peritoneal dialysis can raise readings by more than one hundred, and has been reported with both strip types.

Across strip types: very high triglycerides take up volume and read low; very high uric acid is oxidised at the electrode and reads high; acetaminophen reads high in some systems; and poor perfusion lowers capillary glucose.
Back to the hook. Anaemia pushes the meter high, so confirm with a laboratory plasma glucose before treating. Bedside glucose is mainly a monitoring tool, not a definitive diagnosis.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “An anaemic patient’s meter reading of 300 is true hyperglycaemia” (✓ low haematocrit tends to read falsely high — confirm with a laboratory plasma glucose); “Supplemental oxygen affects every meter” (✓ oxygen interferes with glucose oxidase strips; dehydrogenase strips are little affected); “Lipaemia makes a meter read high” (✓ very high triglycerides take up volume and give falsely LOW meter readings).

cues.text: Trap one: an anaemic patient’s meter reading of three hundred is true hyperglycaemia. No: low haematocrit tends to read falsely high, so confirm in the laboratory.
Trap two: supplemental oxygen affects every meter. No: oxygen interferes with glucose oxidase strips; dehydrogenase strips are little affected.
Trap three: lipaemia makes the meter read high. No: very high triglycerides take up volume and give falsely low readings.

props.title: ✗ “Anaemic + meter 300 = true high.”
lines: ✓ Low Hct reads high; confirm in lab

scenes.title: Crowded strip, quiet signal
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Crowded strip, quiet signal; empty strip, loud signal” — many red cells (high haematocrit) → meter reads LOW; few red cells (anaemia) → meter reads HIGH. Second token: “340 lights up when NADH is made” for the hexokinase method. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: crowded strip, quiet signal; empty strip, loud signal. Many red cells, the meter reads low. Few red cells, the meter reads high. And in the laboratory, three-forty lights up when NADH is made.

Where it breaks: red cells act through several mechanisms, not just crowding; haematocrit-correcting meters shrink the effect; and oxygen, sugars and drugs push readings either way regardless of haematocrit.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Laboratory: hexokinase makes NADH → absorbance rises at 340 nm”, “Meter: low haematocrit reads high, high haematocrit reads low → confirm in the laboratory”.

cues.text: The laboratory measures glucose as a rise in NADH absorbance at 340 nanometres, while a bedside meter reads whole blood and can be fooled by haematocrit, oxygen, sugars and drugs, so confirm a surprising meter value in the laboratory.

props.label: Meter: low Hct high · high Hct low → confirm in lab

explanation.what: Plain language: the laboratory turns glucose into a light-absorbance signal — each glucose molecule makes one molecule that absorbs ultraviolet light at 340 nm. A bedside meter instead runs whole blood over an enzyme strip that makes a tiny current, and the number of red cells, the oxygen level and some sugars and drugs can push that current up or down. Scientific terms: NADH/NAD+, absorbance at 340 nm, hexokinase, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD), glucose oxidase (GOx), glucose dehydrogenase (GDH), electrochemical biosensor, haematocrit (Hct), plasma-equivalent glucose, icodextrin, continuous glucose monitor (CGM).
explanation.why: NADH absorbs at 340 nm and NAD+ does not, so the NADH made in the coupled hexokinase/G6PD reaction measures glucose directly. Meters measure whole blood and convert to plasma-equivalent values, yet many remain affected by haematocrit; red cells contain glucose and can block the electrode or enzyme. Oxygen competes with the mediator on glucose oxidase strips; other sugars can react on dehydrogenase strips; triglycerides take up volume; uric acid and acetaminophen can be oxidised at the electrode.
explanation.measure: Hexokinase method: NADH formed is equimolar to glucose, read at 340 nm. Plasma glucose is about 10–15% higher than whole-blood glucose. Haematocrit below about 35% tends to give too-high meter readings; high haematocrit too-low readings (example: up to +18 mg/dL at true 80 mg/dL and Hct 0.25). GOx strips: high pO2 → low, low pO2 → high. Icodextrin can raise readings by more than 100 mg/dL.
explanation.differs: Laboratory hexokinase (plasma, absorbance rise at 340 nm, a reference method) vs bedside meter (whole blood, electrochemical, interference-prone); glucose oxidase (oxygen-sensitive) vs glucose dehydrogenase (little oxygen effect, other-sugar interference).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: the direction of meter error in anaemia or polycythaemia, which strip chemistry is oxygen-sensitive, whether NADH rises or falls at 340 nm in the hexokinase method, and the next step for a surprising bedside value (confirm with a laboratory plasma glucose).

mnemonic.explanation: Fixes the direction of the haematocrit effect and the direction of the 340 nm change in the hexokinase method.
mnemonic.limitation: Red cells act through several mechanisms, not just crowding; haematocrit-correcting meters reduce the effect; oxygen, other sugars and drugs push readings either way independently of haematocrit.

The size of interferences differs between meter models.

questions.stem: In the hexokinase/glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase method for glucose, what is measured at 340 nm as glucose concentration increases?

options.text: An increase in absorbance as NADH is formed
options.rationale: Correct. One NADH is formed per glucose converted, and NADH absorbs at 340 nm.

options.text: A decrease in absorbance as NADH is consumed
options.rationale: Incorrect. In this method the cofactor is reduced, not oxidised, so absorbance rises.

options.text: An increase in absorbance as NAD+ is formed
options.rationale: Incorrect. NAD+ does not absorb at 340 nm.

options.text: A change in electrode current from hydrogen peroxide
options.rationale: Incorrect. The hexokinase method is photometric: it is read as light absorbance at 340 nm, not as an electrode current.

questions.stem: A patient with polycythaemia (haematocrit 62%) has a bedside meter glucose and a simultaneous laboratory plasma glucose. On a meter without haematocrit correction, the meter result is most likely:

options.text: Falsely low compared with the laboratory value
options.rationale: Correct. High haematocrit is associated with lower meter readings.

options.text: Falsely high compared with the laboratory value
options.rationale: Incorrect. Falsely high readings are associated with low haematocrit (anaemia).

options.text: Identical, because meters report plasma-equivalent values
options.rationale: Incorrect. Many meters remain affected by haematocrit despite reporting plasma-equivalent values.

options.text: Unaffected, because haematocrit only affects photometric methods
options.rationale: Incorrect. The haematocrit effect is a whole-blood meter problem.

questions.stem: A patient on high-flow oxygen is monitored with a glucose oxidase-based meter. Which error is most likely from the oxygen?

options.text: Falsely low readings, because oxygen competes with the mediator for electrons
options.rationale: Correct. On glucose oxidase strips, high oxygen can give falsely low results.

options.text: Falsely high readings, because oxygen is oxidised at the electrode
options.rationale: Incorrect. Falsely high readings are linked to low oxygen tension on these strips.

options.text: No error, because oxygen affects only glucose dehydrogenase strips
options.rationale: Incorrect. It is the reverse: dehydrogenase strips are little affected by oxygen.

options.text: Falsely high readings from maltose cross-reactivity
options.rationale: Incorrect. Maltose interference is mainly a glucose dehydrogenase strip problem and is unrelated to oxygen.

claims.text: NADH absorbs at 340 nm; NAD+ does not.
Hexokinase/G6PD reaction forms NADH equimolar to glucose, read as a 340 nm increase; central-laboratory hexokinase as a reference method for meters.
Plasma ~10–15% higher than whole blood; most meters convert to plasma-equivalent values; POCT primarily for monitoring rather than definitive diagnosis (one evaluation).
Low haematocrit → falsely high, high haematocrit → falsely low; RBC glucose and electrode blocking; +18 mg/dL example; correcting meters less susceptible.
Oxygen interference on glucose oxidase strips (high O2 low, low O2 high); GDH little affected; other sugars compete on GDH; icodextrin raises readings (both strip types reported).
Triglycerides → low; very high uric acid → high; acetaminophen → high in some systems and older CGMs; hypoperfusion → low.

Reviewer items not taught: NADPH at 340 nm; 340 nm-decrease assays (ammonia, urea, ALT, AST); lactate, triglyceride and CK variants; tetrazolium/formazan at ~500 nm; calibrating personal meters against simultaneous lab values.
claims.note: No open source read in this session supports these specific statements.

claims.text: Scenario invented; spectrum and strip drawings schematic.

accuracyFlags.issue: The reviewer lists high O2 as giving falsely low POCT glucose without naming the strip chemistry. Erbach 2016 and Ginsberg 2009 attribute oxygen interference to glucose oxidase strips; glucose dehydrogenase strips are little affected.

The reviewer states acetaminophen causes markedly false-positive CGM readings. Interference is system-dependent: a newer CGM with a permselective membrane showed a mean effect of 3.1 mg/dL after 1 g (Calhoun 2018, manufacturer-affiliated).

The reviewer explains the haematocrit effect as RBCs occluding the strip and anaemia letting extra plasma through. Sources read support the direction of error but describe several mechanisms (red cell glucose content, cells blocking the electrode or enzyme, among others) and do not state the reviewer’s plasma-flow explanation.
